title: CS amp, diode-connected load
description: Common-source stage with a diode-connected transistor as the load. The load's low-impedance $\approx 1/g_m$ sets a gain that is a ratio of transconductances, $A_v = g_{m,in}/(g_{m,load} + g_{ds,in} + g_{ds,load})$, which is well-controlled across process and temperature - the classic teaching load. Both devices are blocks (pick the load's device from a table of the opposite polarity): the input device is sized first, from the bandwidth spec, and the load reads the current it lands on, so the branch current is typed once. Because the load is diode-connected, its drain-source voltage equals its own gate-source voltage, so its givens and its wiring declare the connection and the table is read along that diagonal - there is no drop to estimate, and no polarity knob to set, since the diagonal follows whichever sign convention the table itself uses. The output DC level sits one load $V_{GS}$ below the supply, and it is the one value the sheet solves: the input device's drain sits there, and the load's drop depends on the current the input device sets, so the engine searches for the level at which the two agree. The input gate is a port: the stage that drives it supplies its signal and its DC level, which is the gate-source voltage the sizing lands on.

params.name: GBW_target
params.note: the bandwidth the input device is sized for: its gm is set to 2*pi*GBW_target*CL times the over-design factor, so this number sets the current. Ten megahertz into 2 pF is the range of a single gain stage biased at tens of microamps. An example, to be replaced with the design's own spec

params.name: Av_target
params.note: a diode load gives a modest, well-controlled gain

params.name: cdd_per_um
params.note: an estimate from simulation on sky130, 0.3 to 0.4 fF per micron of drain width; no table carries a drain capacitance column

params.name: gbw_margin
params.note: over-design factor on gm for parasitics and PVT

params.name: gm_id
params.note: input inversion: high = efficient/slow, low = fast/thirsty

params.name: gm_id_load
params.note: load inversion: lower gm/ID gives a higher gain (smaller load gm) but costs the output more headroom and adds noise

params.name: V_out
params.note: output DC level, one diode drop below the supply, and the one value this sheet solves. Solved, not set: the input device's drain-source voltage is this level, the diode load carries the current that device sets, and the load's own gate-source voltage at that current puts the output one drop below the supply. The engine searches for the level at which the two agree; the stored value is never read. The search range is the circuit's: the output lies between its two neighbours, ground and the 1.8 V supply, and where the supply moves the wiring reads the range from the wires themselves (the load's source is on vdd)

doc.title: Common-source input device
doc.description: The input device. Its transconductance is set from the bandwidth spec and its inversion level by the efficiency knob, so the branch current follows from the two, and the diode-connected device in series reads that current. Its drain is the output, one gate-source drop of that device below the supply. It exposes its transconductance, output conductance, drain current, gate capacitance, channel-noise density and width.

checks.note: gm/ID cannot exceed the weak-inversion ceiling of the data

doc.title: Diode-connected load device
doc.description: One device diode-connected (gate tied to drain), so its vds equals its vgs. Carries the stage current, exposing its transconductance (which sets the gain and the output level), its output conductance, its gate-source drop and its width.

equations.name: Rout
equations.note: the resistance this stage presents at its output: the diode load's own transconductance dominates it — both output conductances add in parallel and move it by under a tenth. The gain assumes a capacitive load, so nothing here models a resistive one; this equation is what a composing parent checks its own loading against

equations.name: Av
equations.note: input gm into the diode load conductance (~load gm) plus both output conductances

equations.name: Cout
equations.note: the load, the diode load's own gate capacitance, since its gate is the output node, and what the two drains add, their junctions and the input device's gate-drain overlap, at cdd_per_um per micron of their widths, so a resized device carries a proportionate estimate. At the defaults on the sky130 tables the table puts 10 fF on the load's gate and the drains add 2.2 fF by this estimate, while the devices add 8.7 fF at the output in all, simulated: the part of the gate's capacitance that is to its own drain sits across the one node and adds nothing. Wiring comes on top, so refine from extraction

equations.name: GBW
equations.note: the gm/ID currency, and a good estimate of the unity-gain frequency only while Av0 is comfortably above 1. A diode load is exactly the regime where it is not: a single-pole stage crosses unity at f_p*sqrt(Av0^2 - 1), so at Av0 near 1.4-1.5 the literal crossing sits 25-30% below this value. Read it as transconductance per load capacitance, not as a measured bandwidth

equations.name: vn_in
equations.note: the diode load's own drain noise (vnth_m_load*gm_load) referred to the input by 1/gm_in

equations.name: cgg_in
equations.note: estimate: the capacitance the input terminal presents — this stage's gate capacitance and nothing else. Gate capacitance only, because the Miller term needs the gate-drain fraction and these tables do not carry it, so a driving stage sees more than this. No check reads it

equations.name: I_q
equations.note: estimate: quiescent supply current — the branch current, which here is an OUTPUT of the sizing rather than a setting: the bandwidth spec fixes gm, and the chosen inversion divides it down to a current. The datasheet line for comparing designs; no check reads it

checks.note: read from the table's own noise where it carries it, and from the γ = 1 estimate otherwise; the simulator owns noise sign-off
actual GBW into CL plus the parasitic estimate; the over-design factor should keep this green
